---
title: "03 — Fabry–Pérot cavity"
---

Different physics: an optical cavity is a single-pole low-pass,

$$G(s) = \frac{\omega_c}{s + \omega_c}$$

with the cavity pole `fc` setting the bandwidth (DC gain 1). There is **no sharp
resonance** to aim at — the identification is **signal-to-noise limited**. The
parameter of interest (`fc`) only bends the shape of `|G(f)|` near the pole,
which here sits at 100 Hz, so the whole rolloff has to be measured cleanly for
the fit to lock onto it. That is a nice contrast to the resonance examples,
where a tall peak hands the estimator a high-SNR target.

We do this the Pintelon–Schoukens way, exactly as in the other examples: drive
a digital twin of the cavity with a **periodic multisine**, take the
**leakage-free reference-based FRF**, and recover the pole by **maximum
likelihood** from a 30 %-wrong prior. Because the pole is at 100 Hz we sample
fast enough (8 kHz) that the measurement band spans a decade either side,
~1 Hz … 1 kHz, with the top of the band still well below Nyquist.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

from system_ident.model import TFModel
from system_ident.plant import SuspensionPlant
from system_ident.backends.twin import TwinBackend
from system_ident.excitation import multisine_from_psd
from system_ident.loop import SysIDLoop
from system_ident.estimators.gml import GMLEstimator

SKY, GOLD, RED, GRAY = '#1F8AC0', '#C8973A', '#E53E3E', '#94A3B8'

FS, NPERSEG, N_PERIODS = 8192.0, 32768, 8    # period = 4 s, 8 periods -> 32 s
TOTAL = NPERSEG * N_PERIODS / FS

fc = 100.0                                   # true cavity pole [Hz]
wc = 2 * np.pi * fc
cavity = TFModel.from_zpk(zeros=[], poles=[-wc], gain=wc)   # DC gain = 1

# Synchronous measurement grid: 1 Hz … 1 kHz on the leakage-free bin lattice.
f_all = np.fft.rfftfreq(NPERSEG, 1 / FS)
band = (f_all >= 1.0) & (f_all <= 1000.0)
freq = f_all[band]
```

## Periodic measurement — multisine + leakage-free FRF

The twin discretises the continuous cavity and filters the drive through it,
adding white sensor noise. We inject a flat-budget Schroeder multisine (a smooth,
bounded, low-crest waveform), read back the drive monitor and the cavity
response, and form the reference-based FRF `H = mean(Y)/mean(X)` over periods —
leakage-free because the drive is periodic over `NPERSEG`.

```{python}
tw = TwinBackend(
    SuspensionPlant({"CAV": cavity}, FS),
    {"C1:EXC": "CAV"}, {"C1:RSP": "CAV"},
    fs=FS, sensor_asd=0.09,                   # white sensor noise -> ~5% FRF scatter near the pole
)

Pxx = np.ones_like(freq)                      # flat in-band budget (the FRF is scale-free)
drive = multisine_from_psd(Pxx, FS, NPERSEG, N_PERIODS, freq, seed=0)
tw.inject("C1:EXC", drive, FS)
seg = tw.read(["C1:EXC", "C1:RSP"], TOTAL)

H, H_err, _ = SysIDLoop._estimate_tf_periodic(
    seg["C1:EXC"], seg["C1:RSP"], FS, NPERSEG, band
)
```

## Is the drive gentle? — the measurement time series

Even for a low-pass with nothing to resonate, the excitation is worth a look:
the drive is a smooth, bounded multisine, and the cavity response is a
low-pass-smoothed version of it — no impulsive kicks, just a steady bounded
oscillation the actuator can live with.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cavity-timeseries
#| fig-cap: "One injection, first ~8 s (2 periods). The drive (top) is a smooth low-crest Schroeder multisine; the cavity response (bottom) is the low-pass-smoothed motion. The drive stays well inside a safe actuator range."

idx = np.arange(0, int(8 * FS), 2)             # first 2 periods, decimated 2x for display
t = idx / FS
fig = make_subplots(
    rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.10,
    subplot_titles=['<b>Drive</b> — cavity actuator (Schroeder multisine)',
                    '<b>Cavity response</b> — single-pole low-pass output'],
)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=seg["C1:EXC"][idx], mode='lines',
              line=dict(color=SKY, width=1.2), name='drive'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=seg["C1:RSP"][idx], mode='lines',
              line=dict(color=GOLD, width=1.4), name='response'), row=2, col=1)
fig.update_layout(template='plotly_white', height=440,
                  margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=50, b=50),
                  font=dict(family='Outfit, Inter, sans-serif', size=12),
                  legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.06, xanchor='right', x=1))
fig.update_yaxes(title_text='drive [cts]', row=1, col=1, gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)')
fig.update_yaxes(title_text='response [a.u.]', row=2, col=1, gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)')
fig.update_xaxes(title_text='time [s]', row=2, col=1, gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)')
fig.show()
```

## Fit the cavity pole by maximum likelihood

```{python}
# Prior: 30% off on the pole location (70 Hz instead of 100 Hz).
prior = TFModel.from_zpk(zeros=[], poles=[-2 * np.pi * 70.0], gain=2 * np.pi * 70.0)
fit = GMLEstimator().fit(freq, H, H_err, prior)

f_pole_prior = abs(prior.den[1]) / (2 * np.pi)
f_pole_fit = abs(fit.den[1]) / (2 * np.pi)
print(f"Prior cavity pole:  {f_pole_prior:.1f} Hz  (30% wrong)")
print(f"True  cavity pole:  {fc:.1f} Hz")
print(f"Fit   cavity pole:  {f_pole_fit:.2f} Hz  (error: {abs(f_pole_fit - fc) / fc * 100:.2f}%)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cavity
#| fig-cap: "Single-pole cavity on a log–log Bode plot: true plant (blue), leakage-free measured points (grey), the 30 %-wrong prior (red dotted), and the ML fit (gold dashed). The fit converges from the 70 Hz prior to the true 100 Hz pole even though the noise grows in the far-from-pole rolloff."

ex = np.isfinite(H_err)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(cavity.eval(freq)), mode='lines',
    line=dict(color=SKY, width=2.5), name=f'True plant  (f_c = {fc:.0f} Hz)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq[ex], y=np.abs(H[ex]), mode='markers',
    marker=dict(color='rgba(148,163,184,0.45)', size=3), name='Measured (multisine FRF)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |Hmeas| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(prior.eval(freq)), mode='lines',
    line=dict(color=RED, width=1.8, dash='dot'),
    name=f'Prior  (f_c = {f_pole_prior:.0f} Hz)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G_prior| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(fit.eval(freq)), mode='lines',
    line=dict(color=GOLD, width=2.2, dash='dash'),
    name=f'Fitted  (f_c = {f_pole_fit:.1f} Hz)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G_fit| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))

fig.add_vline(x=fc, line_color='rgba(31,138,192,0.35)', line_dash='dot', line_width=1.5)
fig.add_annotation(
    x=np.log10(fc), y=0.0, xref='x', yref='paper',
    text=f'<b>f_c = {fc:.0f} Hz</b>',
    showarrow=False, xanchor='left', yanchor='bottom',
    font=dict(size=11, color=SKY, family='Outfit, sans-serif'),
    xshift=8, yshift=6,
)
fig.update_layout(
    template='plotly_white', height=400,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=20, b=55),
    font=dict(family='Outfit, Inter, sans-serif', size=12),
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.02, xanchor='right', x=1,
                bgcolor='rgba(255,255,255,0.9)', bordercolor='#DCE5F0', borderwidth=1),
    xaxis=dict(title='Frequency  [Hz]', type='log', gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)'),
    yaxis=dict(title='|G(f)|', type='log', gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)'),
)
fig.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Log-frequency view of a single-pole system

For a single-pole system the interesting structure — the bend at `fc` — spans
roughly a decade around the pole, so we view it on a **log frequency axis**: the
pole region fills the plot instead of being crushed against the left edge. The
periodic FRF is necessarily measured on the *linear* synchronous bin lattice
(`k·fs/NPERSEG`), which is what makes it leakage-free; the densely-sampled
high-frequency rolloff is also the **noisiest** part, since `|G|` is small there.
That is fine: `GMLEstimator` weights every bin by its measured variance
(`H_err`), so the noisy far-from-pole bins are automatically down-weighted and
the fit is dominated by the well-measured region around the pole.
:::
